summary: An IMF Chart of the Week blog post by P. Bhanumati, Mark de Haan and James William Tebrake, dated June 30, 2022, reports that global greenhouse gas emissions fell 4.6 percent in 2020 during pandemic lockdowns but rebounded 6.4 percent in 2021 to a new record above pre-pandemic peaks. It attributes the largest recent increases to manufacturing and energy sectors, notes that omicron-related health measures temporarily reduced household and electricity emissions, and cites IPCC guidance that emissions must peak by 2025 to limit warming to about 1.5 degrees Celsius.
one_line: IMF blog post reporting that global greenhouse gas emissions rebounded 6.4 percent in 2021 to a record, erasing the 2020 pandemic drop.
key_facts: Emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases plunged 4.6 percent in 2020 as lockdowns in the first half of the year restricted global mobility and hampered economic activity.
Annual global greenhouse gas emissions rebounded 6.4 percent in 2021 to a new record, eclipsing the pre-pandemic peak as global economic activity resumed.
The IMF's Climate Change Indicators Dashboard is a joint effort among national and international statistical organizations to provide timely data to help monitor the transition to lower carbon use.
Emissions from the manufacturing and the energy sectors contributed the most to recent global increases, according to the IMF's Climate Change Indicators Dashboard.
Increases from transportation and households were more muted in 2021 as the pandemic weighed on global mobility.
The emergence of the omicron variant in the fourth quarter of 2021 led public health policy measures in many countries to drive down emissions of households and of the electricity sector.
The authors say it will be important to monitor household and electricity sector emissions as economies fully reopen amid historically high fossil fuel-based energy prices.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has said that limiting atmospheric warming to around 1.5 degrees Celsius requires global greenhouse gas emissions to peak by 2025 at the latest.
The post's authors are P. Bhanumati, Mark de Haan and James William Tebrake.
The blog post was published June 30, 2022 in the IMF blog's Chart of the Week series under the Climate change topic.
